issues.legal_issue: A second appellate court may call for a finding on effective possession when the first appellate court has not decided a crucial factual question bearing on possessory title.
material_facts: Both sides lacked established legal title and relied on possessory title.

The trial court considered evidence about whether tenants had paid rent to the persons claiming through them, but the first appellate court relied on the tenants’ written acknowledgment without deciding the rent question.
The High Court called for a finding on whether the tenants had really attorned, and the further finding supported the earlier possession of the plaintiff.
issues.conclusion: The High Court was justified in calling for a finding because the first appellate court had not decided the crucial question of effective possession after considering the rent evidence.
issues.legal_principle: A second appellate court cannot interfere with a finding of fact merely because it would scrutinise the evidence differently. It may, however, call for a finding where the first appellate court has not decided a crucial factual question. The majority cited no statutory provision or earlier case for this holding; Justice Raghubar Dayal disagreed with the majority’s treatment of the High Court’s order and considered that mere failure to scrutinise evidence as the High Court desired did not justify interference.

predicates.second_appeal: A party appealed from a decision made by a first appellate court to a second appellate court.
predicates.possessory_title_dispute: The parties disputed who had the better right to possession despite neither establishing legal title.
predicates.first_appellate_court_relied_on_attornme: The first appellate court relied on a document by which tenants purported to acknowledge a claimant as landlord.
predicates.first_appellate_court_omitted_rent_evide: The first appellate court did not decide the material question whether the tenants paid rent to the claimant.

issues.definition: When a possessory-title dispute reaches a second appeal and the first appellate court relies on an attornment document without deciding material rent evidence, the second appellate court may call for a finding on effective possession.

issues.legal_issue: A paper attornment by tenants does not establish effective possession for a claimant without title unless the tenants pay rent to that claimant voluntarily or under a decree.
material_facts: Neither side established legal title to the property.
The claimants said they had obtained possession through tenants who had previously occupied the property under an earlier tenancy.
The tenants signed a document in favour of the claimants, but the trial court found that they paid no rent to them and that no rent decree had been obtained.
The plaintiff later obtained possession through a tenant before being dispossessed by the opposing claimants.
issues.conclusion: The majority held that the paper attornment did not establish effective possession for the claimants because the tenants had paid no rent to them and no decree for rent had been obtained.
issues.legal_principle: Where a person without title relies on possessory title through tenants, a mere paper attornment is insufficient against third parties; effective possession requires that the tenants pay rent to that person voluntarily or under a decree. The majority cited no statutory provision or earlier case for this rule. Justice Raghubar Dayal dissented from the rent-payment requirement for a genuine attornment.

issues.legal_issue: A genuine agreement by tenants to recognise a claimant as landlord constitutes effective attornment without requiring payment of rent.
material_facts: The case concerned rival claims to possessory title, with neither side establishing legal title.
Justice Raghubar Dayal considered the effect of a tenant’s agreement to accept a person claiming through the previous landlord as the new landlord.
He considered that such an agreement, if it was genuine attornment, would be effective without subsequent payment of rent.
issues.conclusion: In dissent, Justice Raghubar Dayal held that genuine attornment is complete when the tenant agrees to recognise the claimant as landlord and does not depend on subsequent payment of rent.
issues.legal_principle: Justice Raghubar Dayal relied on paragraphs 732 and 745–747 of Foa’s General Law of Landlord and Tenant, section 116 of the Indian Evidence Act, and Krishna Prasad Lal Singha Deo v. Baraboni Coal Concern, (1937) L.R. 64 I.A. 311. He considered attornment a recognition of the new landlord that is complete upon agreement, while noting that the document in this case was not, in his view, an attornment.

issues.definition: In a possessory-title dispute, a genuine agreement by a tenant to recognise a claimant as landlord establishes possession through the tenant without requiring rent payment.

issues.legal_issue: A document creating a fresh tenancy on materially different terms is not an attornment, and a fresh lease granted by persons without title creates no right in the property.
material_facts: The document relied on by the claimants extended the tenancy beyond the unexpired term of the earlier tenancy, covered additional land, and set a different, reduced rent.
The persons granting the purported new lease had no title to the property and had not themselves been in actual possession.
Justice Raghubar Dayal considered that the tenants’ possession remained traceable to the earlier tenancy rather than to a tenancy created by the claimants.
issues.conclusion: In his separate opinion, Justice Raghubar Dayal held that the document was a fresh lease rather than an attornment, and that it created no right or possession for the claimants because its grantors had no title.
issues.legal_principle: Justice Raghubar Dayal distinguished an attornment, which recognises a new landlord under the existing tenancy, from a fresh lease on materially different terms. A person without title cannot create rights in the property by granting a new lease. He relied on the discussion of attornment in Foa’s General Law of Landlord and Tenant and referred to section 116 of the Indian Evidence Act and Krishna Prasad Lal Singha Deo v. Baraboni Coal Concern, (1937) L.R. 64 I.A. 311, in addressing tenant recognition and estoppel.

issues.definition: When a document materially changes an existing tenancy and is granted by a person without title, it is a fresh lease that creates no right or possession for that grantor.
